short: The business of helping companies and governments raise money from investors and advising them on buying, selling or merging businesses.
kid: When a big shop wants to buy another shop, or needs coins from lots of people to grow, it asks special helpers who know how to arrange it. These helpers are like matchmakers for grown-up businesses.
detail: Investment banking is the part of finance that helps companies, governments and funds raise capital and carry out large corporate transactions. Its two core jobs are advisory, such as guiding a client through a merger, acquisition or restructuring, and capital markets, which means underwriting and selling new shares (IPOs, QIPs) and bonds to investors. Banks earn mostly fees, not interest. Many also run sales, trading and research desks that serve institutional investors. In India, a firm that manages a public issue must be registered with SEBI as a merchant banker, and in an IPO it acts as a book running lead manager. The common confusion is with commercial banking: a commercial bank takes deposits and makes loans, while an investment bank arranges and advises on deals and is paid for that work rather than for lending.
example: Say XYZ Ltd wants to raise ₹1,000 crore in an IPO. It hires two investment banks as lead managers and agrees a fee of 2% of the issue, so total fees are ₹20 crore, split between them. In return the banks prepare the offer document, market the shares to investors and help set the price.

short: The informal name for the largest global investment banks, which handle the biggest deals and offer every service from advice to trading and lending.
kid: In the playground a few of the biggest kids can carry the heaviest boxes and help with any game. Everyone calls them first for the giant jobs.
detail: Bulge bracket is the informal label for the handful of largest full-service investment banks that dominate global league tables for M&A advice and for equity and debt underwriting. The group usually named includes Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, JPMorgan, Bank of America and Citi, with some lists adding a few others; membership is not official and shifts over time. The name comes from tombstone advertisements for securities offerings, where the leading underwriters' names were printed first and in larger type, so they bulged out. These banks combine advisory with large balance sheets, trading desks and global reach, which lets them underwrite huge issues and offer financing alongside advice. In India they work alongside large domestic investment banks on big IPOs and cross-border deals. Do not read bulge bracket as best: elite boutiques often win the top advisory mandates.
example: Say a $10 billion cross-border acquisition needs both advice and $6 billion of loan financing. A bulge bracket bank can advise and also arrange the loan from its own balance sheet, while a boutique could only advise. At an advisory fee of 0.2% of deal value, the advice alone is worth $20 million.

short: A smaller investment bank that focuses on giving advice, mainly on mergers, acquisitions and restructuring, rather than lending, trading or selling new securities.
kid: Instead of a giant supermarket that sells everything, this is a small shop that only makes the best cakes. People come because it is very good at one thing.
detail: A boutique investment bank is an advisory-focused firm without a large balance sheet, trading floor or underwriting business. Its work is mainly advising on M&A, restructuring, capital-raising strategy and fundraising for private companies, often within one sector or region. Elite boutiques such as Evercore, Lazard, Centerview and PJT Partners compete head to head with bulge bracket banks for the largest M&A mandates. Boutiques present themselves as independent: because they do not lend or trade, they face fewer conflicts of interest, and senior bankers stay closely involved. The trade-off is that they cannot offer financing alongside their advice. In India, many mid-market boutiques advise on private equity rounds, sales of family businesses and cross-border deals. Do not assume small means minor: top boutiques regularly advise on deals worth tens of billions of dollars.
example: Say ABC Ltd sells its packaging business for ₹800 crore and pays its boutique adviser a success fee of 1.5%. If the deal closes, the boutique earns ₹12 crore; if it fails, the boutique may earn only a small monthly retainer.

short: Rules and systems inside a financial firm that stop confidential deal information held by one team from reaching other teams that could misuse it.
kid: If you know about a surprise party, you keep the secret in your room and do not tell the friends next door. A wall like that keeps secrets where they belong.
detail: A Chinese wall is a set of procedures that separates people holding unpublished price-sensitive information from those who trade, advise investors or publish research. In an investment bank, the M&A team working on a confidential takeover sits on the private side, while traders, sales staff and research analysts sit on the public side. Walls rely on separate offices and IT access, restricted and watch lists, monitored communications and compliance approval before anyone is brought over the wall. They matter because trading on inside information is insider trading. In India, SEBI's Prohibition of Insider Trading Regulations require listed companies and intermediaries to maintain such barriers and a structured digital database of who holds sensitive information. Some firms now prefer the terms information barrier or ethical wall. A wall does not remove conflicts of interest; it only manages them.
example: Say a bank is advising ABC Ltd on a secret bid for XYZ Ltd at ₹250 a share, while XYZ trades at ₹200. That is a 25% premium, so a trader who bought 10,000 XYZ shares early would gain ₹5 lakh when the bid is announced. The Chinese wall exists to stop that information ever reaching the trading desk.

short: A slide presentation an investment bank uses to win a client's business, showing market views, valuation ideas, deal suggestions and the bank's track record.
kid: Before helping with a big job, the helpers show a picture book about what they would do and why they are good at it. They hope it makes you pick them.
detail: A pitch book is the presentation bankers prepare for a meeting with a current or prospective client. A typical book covers the bank's credentials and league table rankings, a view of the client's industry and share price, valuation analysis using comparable companies, precedent transactions and DCF, and specific ideas such as acquisition targets, a sale process, a fundraise or an IPO. Junior analysts and associates spend much of their time building, checking and formatting these books, which is why the word has become shorthand for the long hours of the job. Pitch books matter because advisory work is won on credibility and ideas long before any fee is earned. Do not confuse a pitch book, which sells the bank to a client, with an information memorandum, which sells the client's business to buyers.
example: Say a bank pitches ABC Ltd on buying a rival. Its pitch book shows the rival's annual profit of ₹100 crore and peer valuations of 15 to 18 times profit, so it suggests an indicative price of ₹1,500 crore to ₹1,800 crore.

short: The buying, selling and combining of companies or their businesses, usually to grow faster, cut costs or reach new products and customers.
kid: Sometimes two lemonade stands decide to join into one, or one stand buys another. Putting businesses together like this, or splitting them apart, is what this is all about.
detail: Mergers and acquisitions is the umbrella term for transactions that change who owns or controls a business. A merger combines two companies into one legal entity; an acquisition is one company buying control of another, through its shares or its assets. The field also covers divestitures, spin-offs, joint ventures and stake sales. Companies pursue M&A for synergies, scale, new markets, technology or talent, and pay with cash, shares or a mix. Investment banks advise on valuation, structure and negotiation, while lawyers, accountants and regulators shape the process. In India, deals pass through the Companies Act, SEBI's takeover code for listed targets, Competition Commission of India approval above size thresholds and NCLT sanction for schemes of merger. Studies repeatedly find that many acquisitions fail to create value for the buyer's shareholders, often because the price paid already gave away the expected gains.
example: Say ABC Ltd buys all of XYZ Ltd for ₹1,000 crore when XYZ's shares were worth ₹800 crore on the market. The extra ₹200 crore is a 25% premium, which ABC hopes to earn back through cost savings and higher sales from the combined business.

short: When two companies combine into a single company, so that the owners of both end up owning the combined business.
kid: Two friends each have a box of toys and pour them into one big box they share. Now there is one box, and both friends own it together.
detail: A merger joins two companies so that only one legal entity remains, or a new one is formed. In a merger by absorption, the target transfers its assets and liabilities to the acquirer and is dissolved; in a consolidation, both fold into a fresh company. Target shareholders usually receive shares of the surviving company at an agreed swap ratio, so they become part-owners rather than simply being paid off, although cash can be part of the deal. Indian law uses the word amalgamation, and a merger is carried out as a scheme of arrangement under the Companies Act, 2013, approved by shareholders and creditors and sanctioned by the NCLT. A well-known example is HDFC Ltd merging into HDFC Bank, effective July 2023. The common confusion: news reports often call a deal a merger when it is really an acquisition, with one side clearly taking control.
example: Say XYZ Ltd merges into ABC Ltd at a swap ratio of 2 ABC shares for every 5 XYZ shares. A shareholder with 1,000 XYZ shares receives 400 ABC shares, and XYZ ceases to exist.

short: When one company buys control of another company, or of its business, which often keeps operating under the buyer's ownership.
kid: A bigger lemonade stand buys a smaller one down the street. The small stand still sells lemonade, but now the big stand is in charge of it.
detail: In an acquisition, the acquirer buys control of a target, either by purchasing its shares (a share deal) or its assets and business (an asset deal). Unlike a merger, the target often survives as a subsidiary, and the deal is paid for in cash, shares or a mix. Control normally means more than 50% of voting rights, though a smaller stake can give control through board seats or special rights. The acquirer usually pays a premium over the market price to persuade owners to sell, and the excess of price paid over the fair value of identifiable net assets is booked as goodwill. In India, under SEBI's takeover code as of 2025, buying 25% or more of a listed company, or acquiring control, triggers a mandatory open offer. Takeover is a common synonym; it can be friendly, agreed with the target's board, or hostile, pursued over the board's objection.
example: Say ABC Ltd buys 60% of XYZ Ltd, whose equity is valued at ₹500 crore, and pays a 20% premium. The stake is worth ₹300 crore at that value, so ABC pays ₹360 crore and XYZ becomes its subsidiary.

short: A merger of two companies of similar size and value, combined on roughly even terms with little or no premium paid to either side.
kid: Two friends with the same number of marbles put them together and agree they are both in charge of the big pile. Neither one is the boss of the other.
detail: A merger of equals combines two firms of broadly similar market value so that each set of shareholders owns about half of the new company. Because neither side is buying the other, the share exchange usually carries little or no control premium, and governance is shared: board seats are split, and the chair and CEO roles are divided or rotated, often with a new name or headquarters. Companies use the structure to gain scale without paying a premium. The label can mislead, however. In practice one side often ends up dominating management, strategy and culture, and the 1998 combination of Daimler-Benz and Chrysler, billed as a merger of equals, became a textbook case of culture clash and failed integration. Analysts therefore look past the name to the ownership split, the board and who holds the top jobs.
example: Say ABC Ltd and XYZ Ltd are each worth ₹10,000 crore. In a merger of equals the combined ₹20,000 crore company is owned 50:50, so each side's shareholders hold half of it and neither receives a premium.

short: A merger between two companies that sell similar products in the same industry and usually compete with each other.
kid: Two ice-cream carts on the same beach decide to become one cart. Now there is one cart instead of two racing for the same customers.
detail: A horizontal merger joins firms at the same stage of the same industry, such as two cement makers, two airlines or two banks. The usual goals are economies of scale, cutting duplicate costs such as plants, offices and marketing, a wider product range or geographic reach, and stronger pricing power. That last point is why horizontal deals attract the closest antitrust scrutiny: removing a competitor raises market concentration, which can lead to higher prices for customers. Regulators assess this with market shares and concentration measures such as the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index, and may block the deal or demand that overlapping businesses be sold. In India, the Competition Commission of India reviews combinations above set size thresholds. Contrast this with a vertical merger, which joins a firm with its supplier or customer, and a conglomerate merger, which joins unrelated businesses.
example: Say ABC Cement and XYZ Cement hold 18% and 12% of a regional market. A horizontal merger would create a firm with a 30% share, so the competition regulator checks whether customers would face higher prices and may ask them to sell some plants.

short: A merger between companies at different steps of the same supply chain, such as a manufacturer combining with its supplier or distributor.
kid: A bakery buys the farm that grows its wheat. Now the bakery gets its own flour instead of buying it from someone else.
detail: A vertical merger joins firms at different steps of making and selling the same product, for example a carmaker buying a parts supplier (backward integration) or a film studio buying a cinema chain or streaming platform (forward integration). The aims are to secure supplies, cut transaction costs and middlemen's margins, coordinate production better and capture more of the profit along the chain. Unlike a horizontal merger, it does not directly remove a competitor, so regulators often view it more favourably. It can still harm competition if the merged firm cuts rivals off from a key input or sales channel, a problem called foreclosure, which competition authorities, including the CCI in India, examine. The business risk is lost flexibility: an owned supplier may become less efficient than shopping around in an open market.
example: Say ABC Foods buys the packaging maker that supplies its cartons. If ABC spends ₹30 crore a year on packaging and the supplier earns a 20% profit margin on those sales, owning the supplier lets ABC keep about ₹6 crore a year, before integration costs.

short: A deal in which a private company becomes listed by merging into an existing listed company, instead of going through a normal IPO.
kid: Instead of building a new shop from scratch, a small business moves into an old shop that already has a sign on the street. Now people can find it straight away.
detail: In a reverse merger, a private operating company merges with a listed company, often a dormant shell with few assets. The private company's owners receive most of the listed company's shares and so take control, even though legally the listed company is the acquirer; hence the name reverse takeover. The appeal is a faster, cheaper route to a listing than an IPO, with no new issue to market. The risk is weaker scrutiny of the business coming in, so regulators demand fresh disclosures, and in India SEBI and the stock exchanges impose conditions when an unlisted company merges into a listed one. The phrase also describes a subsidiary absorbing its parent. Separately, Indian startups use reverse flip for moving their holding company from abroad back to India, often by merging the foreign parent into the Indian unit.
example: Say listed shell ABC Ltd has 1 crore shares and issues 9 crore new shares to the owners of private XYZ Pvt Ltd in exchange for their company. XYZ's owners now hold 9 crore of the 10 crore shares, or 90%, and control the listed company.

short: An attempt to buy control of a company against the wishes of its board, usually by going straight to its shareholders.
kid: Someone wants to buy the class toy box, but the teacher says no. So they ask each child directly to sell their toys to them instead.
detail: A hostile takeover happens when a bidder seeks control of a target whose board rejects, or is never asked about, the approach. The bidder can make a tender or open offer directly to shareholders, buy shares in the market, or run a proxy fight to replace directors with ones who will approve the deal. Targets defend with poison pills, staggered boards, a friendly white knight, or by arguing the price is too low. Hostile bids are more common in the US and UK, where ownership is widely dispersed. They are rare in India because most listed companies have promoters holding large controlling stakes; L&T's acquisition of Mindtree in 2019 is the best-known exception. A corporate raider is an investor known for hostile bids. Note that an unsolicited bid is not automatically hostile: it becomes hostile only when the board opposes it and the bidder presses on.
example: Say XYZ Ltd trades at ₹400 and its board rejects a ₹480 offer from ABC Ltd. ABC then offers ₹480 a share directly to shareholders, a 20% premium, and if holders of 51% of the shares accept, ABC gains control despite the board.

short: A public offer to buy shares directly from a company's shareholders at a fixed price, usually above the market price, for a limited time.
kid: A kid tells the whole class, 'I will give two sweets for every sticker you bring me by Friday.' Anyone who likes the deal can hand over their stickers.
detail: A tender offer invites all shareholders of a company to sell some or all of their shares to the bidder at a stated price within a stated window. The price is usually at a premium to the market, and the offer is often conditional on receiving a minimum number of shares, such as enough for control. Bidders use it to win control quickly, including in hostile situations, because it goes around the board. Companies also use tender offers to buy back their own shares. In the US, tender offers follow SEC rules on disclosure and timing. In India the takeover equivalent is the open offer under SEBI's takeover code, and under SEBI's buyback rules as of 2025, listed companies buy back shares mainly through a tender offer route. Do not confuse it with a government tender, which is a bidding process for contracts.
example: Say ABC Inc's shares trade at $40 and a bidder offers $50 per share for up to 10 million shares. That is a 25% premium, and if the offer is fully accepted the bidder pays $500 million.

short: In India, an offer an acquirer must make to buy shares from a listed company's public shareholders after crossing set ownership or control thresholds.
kid: If a new kid buys a big part of the class toy box, the rule says every other kid must get a fair chance to sell their toys to the new kid too. Nobody has to sell, but everyone gets the same chance.
detail: An open offer is the mechanism under SEBI's Substantial Acquisition of Shares and Takeovers Regulations, 2011, that gives public shareholders an exit when control of a listed company changes. Under the rules as of 2025, it is triggered when an acquirer, together with persons acting in concert, reaches 25% of voting rights, buys more than 5% in a financial year while holding between 25% and the maximum permitted non-public holding, or acquires control. The offer must be for at least 26% of the total shares, at a price no lower than the highest of several benchmarks, including the highest price the acquirer has paid and recent market averages. Its purpose is fairness: minority holders should share in any control premium. Shareholders may accept or keep their shares. It resembles a tender offer, but it is mandatory and its terms are set by regulation.
example: Say ABC Ltd buys 30% of listed XYZ Ltd, which has 10 crore shares, at ₹150 a share. It must then make an open offer for at least 26%, or 2.6 crore shares, and at ₹150 a share full acceptance would cost ₹390 crore.

short: A defence a company's board adopts against a hostile takeover, making it far more expensive for a bidder to build a controlling stake.
kid: If someone tries to grab all the marbles, a rule says every other child instantly gets lots of extra marbles. Now grabbing them all becomes far too hard.
detail: A poison pill, formally a shareholder rights plan, gives existing shareholders the right to buy extra shares at a steep discount if any investor crosses an ownership trigger, often 10% to 20%, without board approval. The hostile bidder is excluded, so its stake is heavily diluted and the cost of control soars. The aim is rarely to block every deal; it forces the bidder to negotiate with the board, buying time to seek a higher price or a white knight. Pills were developed in the US in the 1980s and remain common there; Twitter adopted one in 2022 when Elon Musk bid for the company. They are largely unavailable in India, where SEBI's takeover code, under the rules as of 2025, limits what a target's board can do during an open offer. Critics argue pills entrench management; supporters say they protect shareholders from coercive low bids.
example: Say a raider buys 15% of ABC Inc, which has 100 million shares, and crosses the pill's trigger. Every other holder can buy one new share at half price for each share held, so up to 85 million new shares appear and the raider's stake falls from 15% to about 8.1% of 185 million shares.

short: A friendly buyer that a takeover target invites to acquire it instead of an unwanted hostile bidder.
kid: A bully wants your toy, so you ask a kind friend you trust to look after it instead. The kind friend is the knight who comes to help.
detail: A white knight is a company or investor that rescues a target from a hostile bidder by making a competing offer the target's board prefers, usually on better terms or with promises to keep management, jobs or the brand. Target shareholders often benefit because a contest pushes the price up. The board still has a duty to get the best value, so it cannot simply hand the company to a white knight at a lower price. A white squire is a milder version: a friendly investor buys a significant minority stake, enough to make a hostile bid harder, without taking control. In the colourful vocabulary of takeovers, the hostile bidder is the black knight and an opportunistic third bidder is a grey knight. In India, SEBI's takeover code allows a competing offer within a set window after the first bidder's detailed public statement.
example: Say a hostile bidder offers $30 a share for ABC Inc and the board finds a white knight willing to pay $34, about 13% more. For a holder of 10,000 shares, the white knight's deal is worth $340,000 against $300,000.

short: A large payout promised to top executives if they lose their jobs after their company is taken over.
kid: A team captain is promised a big bag of sweets if a new team takes over and he stops being captain. It makes leaving much softer.
detail: A golden parachute is a clause in a senior executive's contract that pays a large sum, often several years of salary and bonus plus early vesting of share awards, if the executive is dismissed or demoted after a change of control. Most now need a double trigger: the takeover happens and the executive then loses the job or role. Supporters say it lets managers judge a bid on its merits without fearing for their jobs, and keeps them in place through a sale. Critics see it as rewarding failure and as a mild takeover defence, since it raises the cost of buying the company. In the US, shareholders get an advisory vote on such payments in mergers, and excess amounts face penalty taxes. In India, the Companies Act restricts payments to directors for loss of office, so such packages are less common and usually smaller.
example: Say the CEO of ABC Inc earns $2 million a year in salary and bonus and has a parachute worth three times that. If she is fired after a takeover she receives $6 million, on top of any shares that vest early.

short: The extra value created when two combined businesses are worth more together than apart, through cost savings or higher sales.
kid: Two friends each build a small sandcastle. Working together with one bucket, they build a castle bigger than both small ones put together.
detail: Synergies are the gains from combining two firms that neither could achieve alone. Cost synergies come from removing duplication: shared offices, merged supply chains, bigger purchasing discounts and fewer overlapping staff. Revenue synergies come from selling more, through cross-selling to each other's customers, wider distribution or stronger pricing. Bankers estimate the yearly run-rate of synergies, subtract one-time integration costs and value what remains, often with a multiple or a DCF. Synergies matter because they are the main justification for paying a takeover premium: if the premium is larger than the value of the synergies, the buyer's shareholders lose. Cost synergies are generally more reliable than revenue synergies, which depend on customer behaviour. The classic trap is overestimating synergies and underestimating integration problems, while negative synergies, such as lost customers or key staff, are often ignored.
example: Say ABC Ltd is worth ₹3,000 crore and XYZ Ltd ₹1,000 crore on their own, and together they would be worth ₹4,500 crore. The synergies are ₹500 crore, so ABC could pay XYZ's owners a premium of up to ₹500 crore before the deal destroys value for its own shareholders.
formula: Synergy value = Value of combined firm - (Value of acquirer + Value of target)

short: A check of whether an acquisition will raise or lower the buyer's earnings per share, its profit for each share, once the deal is done.
kid: You and your friends share a bag of sweets. If a new friend joins and brings lots of sweets, everyone gets more; if they bring only a few, everyone gets fewer.
detail: Accretion dilution analysis compares the acquirer's earnings per share before a deal with its pro forma EPS after combining both companies' profits and allowing for how the deal is paid for. A deal is accretive if pro forma EPS is higher and dilutive if it is lower. The key drivers are the price paid, the target's earnings and the funding mix: new shares increase the share count, new debt adds interest, and using cash gives up interest income, all after tax. Expected synergies and new amortisation charges are then added in. A quick rule: an all-stock deal is accretive when the acquirer's P/E is higher than the P/E it pays for the target. Markets watch EPS closely, but an accretive deal can still destroy value if it earns less than the cost of capital, and a dilutive one can create value over time.
example: Say ABC Ltd earns ₹100 crore on 10 crore shares, an EPS of ₹10, with its share price at ₹200. It buys XYZ Ltd, which earns ₹20 crore, for ₹300 crore paid by issuing 1.5 crore new shares. Pro forma EPS is ₹120 crore / 11.5 crore shares = ₹10.43, so the deal is about 4.3% accretive.
formula: Pro forma EPS = (Acquirer net income + Target net income + After-tax synergies - After-tax cost of funding) / (Acquirer shares + New shares issued); Accretion or dilution = Pro forma EPS / Acquirer standalone EPS - 1

short: The number of the buyer's shares a target shareholder receives for each target share held, when a deal is paid for in shares.
kid: You trade your toy cars for a friend's stickers and agree that every 2 cars get you 3 stickers. That agreement tells everyone exactly how to swap.
detail: The swap ratio, or exchange ratio, sets how many shares of the acquiring or surviving company are issued for each share of the target in a share-funded merger or amalgamation. It comes from the relative value per share of the two companies, usually a weighted blend of methods such as market price, DCF and asset value, supported by independent valuers and fairness opinions. A fixed ratio means target holders bear the risk of the acquirer's share price moving before closing; some deals use a floating ratio or a collar to share that risk. In India, a scheme of amalgamation states the swap ratio and needs a registered valuer's report and, for listed companies, a fairness opinion and stock exchange clearance before NCLT approval. Note that the ratio, not the headline deal value, decides the ownership split: a ratio favouring the target means more dilution for the acquirer's shareholders.
example: Say ABC Ltd's shares are worth ₹500 and XYZ Ltd's ₹200. The swap ratio is 200 / 500 = 0.4, or 2 ABC shares for every 5 XYZ shares, so a holder of 1,000 XYZ shares receives 400 ABC shares.
formula: Swap ratio = Value per share of target / Value per share of acquirer

short: The detailed investigation a buyer or investor carries out on a business before a deal, to check its facts, risks and value.
kid: Before you swap your bike for a friend's scooter, you check the wheels, brakes and bell carefully. You want to be sure it works the way your friend said.
detail: Due diligence is the structured review of a target before signing or closing a transaction. Financial diligence tests the quality of earnings, working capital, debt and cash flow; legal diligence checks contracts, ownership of assets, licences, litigation and regulatory compliance; tax, commercial, technical, HR, IT and ESG reviews are added as needed. Advisers work through a virtual data room of documents provided by the seller, plus management meetings and site visits. Findings feed directly into the price, the warranties and indemnities, the conditions to closing and sometimes the decision to walk away. Sellers increasingly commission vendor due diligence to speed up auctions. The term also covers underwriters' checks before an IPO; in India the lead managers must give SEBI a due diligence certificate. Do not treat it as box-ticking: problems missed before closing become the buyer's problems afterwards.
example: Say a buyer agrees in principle to pay ₹600 crore for XYZ Ltd, valuing its ₹60 crore of annual profit at 10 times. Due diligence finds ₹6 crore of that profit came from a one-off land sale, so normal profit is ₹54 crore and the same multiple gives ₹540 crore, a ₹60 crore lower price.

short: A short document in which a buyer sets out the main terms it proposes for a deal, before the detailed contracts are negotiated.
kid: Before swapping toys, you write a little note saying you would like to trade your robot for your friend's train. It shows you are serious, but the real swap happens later.
detail: A letter of intent, a close cousin of a term sheet or memorandum of understanding, records the key proposed terms of a transaction: price or valuation range, structure, form of payment, main conditions, timetable and the due diligence the buyer needs. Most of it is non-binding, so either side can walk away, but some clauses usually are binding, such as confidentiality, exclusivity for a set period, governing law and who bears costs. In an auction, bidders first submit indicative, non-binding offers based on the information memorandum; shortlisted bidders then carry out due diligence and submit binding offers. An LOI matters because it frames the negotiation and often grants the buyer exclusivity. In Indian market news, an LoI often means a client's letter awarding a contract, a related but different use. The trap is treating an announced LOI as a done deal; many never reach a signed agreement.
example: Say ABC Ltd signs an LOI to buy XYZ Ltd for ₹450 crore to ₹500 crore, subject to due diligence, with 60 days of exclusivity. After diligence it offers ₹470 crore in the binding agreement, inside the range, but it could have walked away at any point in those 60 days.

short: A detailed document prepared by a seller's adviser describing a business for sale, sent to serious buyers after they sign a confidentiality agreement.
kid: When you want to swap your toy castle, you make a little book with pictures of every room and tower. Only friends who promise to keep it secret get to see it.
detail: An information memorandum, or confidential information memorandum (CIM), is the main marketing document in a sell-side process. It covers the company's history, products, customers, market, management, operations, past financials and often projections, plus the investment highlights the seller wants buyers to notice. The adviser first sends a short, often anonymous teaser of one or two pages to a long list of potential buyers; those interested sign a non-disclosure agreement and receive the IM, which they use to make indicative offers. Detailed due diligence follows for a shortlist. An IM is written to sell, so its projections are the seller's view and buyers must test them. Arrangers of syndicated loans also send an information memorandum to potential lenders. Do not confuse an IM with a prospectus, which is a regulated disclosure document for offering securities to the public.
example: Say an adviser sends a teaser for XYZ Pvt Ltd to 40 possible buyers. Fifteen sign NDAs and receive the IM, 6 submit indicative offers and 3 are shortlisted for due diligence, so 7.5% of those first contacted reach the final round.

short: A contract clause letting a buyer or lender walk away if something seriously harms the target's business between signing and closing.
kid: You agree to buy a friend's bike next week. If it gets badly broken before then, you are allowed to say no thanks.
detail: A material adverse change, or material adverse effect, clause appears in acquisition agreements and loan documents. It lets the buyer refuse to close if, after signing, an event has a significant and lasting negative impact on the target's business, finances or prospects. Sellers negotiate carve-outs so that general risks, such as economy-wide downturns, industry changes, new laws or pandemics, do not count unless they hit the target disproportionately. Courts set a high bar: the harm usually has to be durable, measured in years rather than a quarter. The best-known case in which a buyer succeeded is Akorn v. Fresenius in Delaware in 2018. MAC disputes surged in 2020 as buyers tried to escape deals during Covid-19. The clause matters because it allocates risk in the gap between signing and closing, which can last months while regulators review a deal. A single bad quarter is not an automatic MAC.
example: Say a buyer signs to acquire XYZ Ltd for ₹2,000 crore, and before closing a regulator bans the product that brings in 70% of XYZ's revenue. That is likely a material adverse change that lets the buyer walk away, whereas a 5% dip in one quarter's sales during a market-wide slowdown usually would not be.

short: An amount one side of a deal agrees to pay the other if it walks away, or the deal fails, for reasons the contract names.
kid: You promise a friend you will swap toys tomorrow. If you change your mind, you agree to give them a sweet to say sorry for wasting their time.
detail: A break-up fee compensates a party for the time, cost and lost opportunities of a deal that does not complete. The standard version is paid by the target to the buyer if the target's board changes its recommendation or accepts a better rival bid; in US public deals it is typically around 2% to 4% of equity value, since a much larger fee could unfairly discourage competing offers. A reverse termination fee runs the other way: the buyer pays the target if the deal fails because it cannot secure financing or regulatory approval. These can be large: after US regulators moved to block AT&T's 2011 bid for T-Mobile USA, AT&T paid a break-up package worth about $4 billion, including $3 billion in cash. In India, such fees appear mostly in private and unlisted deals. The fee is owed only for the triggers the contract names.
example: Say ABC Inc agrees to be bought for $5 billion with a 3% break-up fee. If its board later accepts a higher rival bid, ABC must pay the original buyer $150 million.
formula: Break-up fee = Agreed fee percentage x Deal equity value

short: A letter from an independent financial adviser saying whether the price or terms of a deal are financially fair to shareholders.
kid: Before swapping your toy, you ask a grown-up who knows about toys whether the swap is fair. You feel safer saying yes once they have checked.
detail: A fairness opinion is a formal letter, backed by valuation analysis, that a board obtains from an investment bank or independent valuer before approving a merger, acquisition, buyback or similar deal. It concludes whether the consideration is fair, from a financial point of view, to the company's shareholders, using methods such as comparable companies, precedent transactions and DCF. It helps directors show they made an informed decision and protects them against claims of breaching their duties. It is not a recommendation on how to vote and does not say the price is the best obtainable. In India, SEBI's rules as of 2025 require listed companies proposing a scheme of arrangement to obtain a fairness opinion from an independent SEBI-registered merchant banker on the valuation and swap ratio. A known criticism: when the opinion comes from the bank earning a success fee on the deal, its independence is doubtful.
example: Say ABC Ltd agrees to buy XYZ Ltd at ₹520 per share. A merchant banker's valuation range for XYZ is ₹480 to ₹540 per share, so its fairness opinion concludes that the price, which lies inside that range, is fair to ABC's shareholders from a financial point of view.

short: The check by competition regulators of whether a merger or acquisition would reduce competition and harm customers, before the deal can be completed.
kid: If the two biggest sweet shops in town want to become one, a grown-up checks first. They make sure sweets will not suddenly cost too much because there is no other shop.
detail: Antitrust review, or merger control, is the process by which competition authorities examine deals above size thresholds before they close. The regulator studies market shares, concentration, barriers to entry and effects on suppliers and customers. It can approve the deal, approve it with remedies such as selling overlapping businesses, or block it. In India, under the rules as of 2025, combinations crossing asset or turnover thresholds, or a deal-value threshold added in 2024, must be notified to and approved by the Competition Commission of India before completion. In the US the FTC and the Justice Department review deals under the Hart-Scott-Rodino Act, and the European Commission handles large EU deals; global deals may need approval in many countries. Timelines and outcomes are a key deal risk, which is why merger agreements include long-stop dates and reverse termination fees. News use of antitrust also covers conduct cases unrelated to mergers.
example: Say two tyre makers with 25% and 15% of the Indian market agree to merge, creating a 40% share. The CCI might approve the deal only if they sell a brand holding 8% of the market, cutting the combined share to 32%.

short: The sale of part or all of an owner's shareholding in a company, either to another investor or on the stock market.
kid: You own half of a lemonade stand with a friend. You sell some of your half to another friend, so now you own a smaller piece.
detail: A stake sale is when a shareholder, such as a promoter, parent company, government or private equity fund, sells some or all of its shares in a company. It can be done privately to a strategic or financial buyer, through block or bulk deals on the stock exchange, or through an offer for sale in an IPO or afterwards. The seller may want cash, to cut debt, to exit an investment or to meet minimum public shareholding rules. Unlike a fresh issue of shares, a stake sale raises no money for the company itself, because the cash goes to the seller. Markets read these sales closely: a promoter selling can signal reduced confidence or simply a need for cash. In India, a buyer whose purchase crosses the takeover code thresholds must make an open offer. When the government sells stakes in public sector companies, the process is called disinvestment.
example: Say a promoter owns 60% of XYZ Ltd, which has 20 crore shares, and sells 10% of the company in a block deal at ₹300 a share. That is 2 crore shares, raising ₹600 crore for the promoter, not for XYZ, and leaving the promoter with 50%.

short: A company that buys another business because it fits its own operations, such as a competitor, supplier or company in a related industry.
kid: A bakery buys a little jam shop because jam goes perfectly with its bread. It wants the shop to help its own business, not to sell it again later.
detail: A strategic buyer is an operating company acquiring a business that fits its existing activities, as opposed to a financial buyer such as a private equity fund. Strategics look for synergies: cost savings, cross-selling, new products, technology, distribution or entry into a new geography. Because they can capture those benefits, they can often justify paying more than a financial buyer, and they usually plan to hold and integrate the business indefinitely rather than exit. They fund deals with cash, debt or their own shares. In auctions, bankers usually approach both strategics and financial sponsors to maximise competition. In Indian disinvestment, a strategic sale means transferring management control to a buyer, as when the government sold Air India to the Tata group in 2022. The trade-offs for sellers: strategic buyers may need antitrust clearance, can take longer to close and may cut overlapping jobs.
example: Say XYZ Ltd earns ₹50 crore a year. A financial buyer bids 10 times profit, or ₹500 crore. A strategic buyer expects ₹10 crore a year of cost savings, values the combined ₹60 crore of profit at the same 10 times and bids up to ₹600 crore.

short: An investor, often a private equity fund, that buys a company to improve it and sell it later at a profit.
kid: Someone buys an old bike, fixes it up and paints it, planning to sell it for more later. They do not want to ride it themselves forever.
detail: A financial buyer, or financial sponsor, acquires companies as investments rather than to fold them into an operating business. The typical example is a private equity fund doing a leveraged buyout, but family offices, sovereign wealth funds and pension funds can act the same way. Without operating synergies, a financial buyer's price is capped by the return it needs, often expressed as a target internal rate of return or a multiple of its money over a holding period of roughly three to seven years. It lifts returns through borrowing, operational improvements, add-on acquisitions and a well-timed exit by sale or IPO. As a result, financial buyers often bid less than strategic buyers, though cheap debt and large funds let them compete. In deal news, sponsor means this kind of investor; do not confuse it with the sponsor of an Indian mutual fund, which is a different role.
example: Say a fund buys XYZ Ltd for ₹1,000 crore, paying ₹400 crore of its own money and borrowing ₹600 crore. Five years later it sells for ₹1,500 crore and repays the ₹600 crore loan, leaving ₹900 crore, or 2.25 times its money (ignoring interest).
formula: Multiple of money = Equity value at exit / Equity invested

short: When a company gets rid of a business unit, subsidiary or major asset by selling it, spinning it off or closing it.
kid: You have too many toys, so you swap your old train set with a friend for some coins. Now you have more room for the toys you really love.
detail: A divestiture is the disposal of part of a company, such as a division, brand, plant or subsidiary. It can be a sale to a strategic or financial buyer, a spin-off to shareholders, an equity carve-out through an IPO, or a closure. Companies divest to sharpen focus on core businesses, raise cash to cut debt, exit weak or non-core units, unlock value the market is overlooking, or meet antitrust conditions on another deal. When a unit is sold, the seller receives cash or other consideration and books a gain or loss on the sale. In India, a whole business can be transferred as a going concern for a lump sum through a slump sale, which has its own tax treatment. The common confusion is with disinvestment, which in India usually means the government selling stakes in public sector companies; divestiture usually describes a company shedding a business.
example: Say ABC Ltd sells its loss-making snacks division for ₹300 crore and uses the cash to repay debt costing 9% a year. That saves ₹27 crore of interest a year and lets management focus on its core beverages business.

short: When a company turns one of its businesses into a separate company and gives the new company's shares to its own shareholders.
kid: A big lemonade stand also sells cookies. One day the cookie table becomes its own stand, and everyone who owned the lemonade stand now owns the cookie stand too.
detail: In a spin-off, a parent company separates a division into a new independent company and distributes the new company's shares to its existing shareholders, usually in proportion to their holdings. No cash changes hands, and both companies then trade separately. Reasons include letting each business follow its own strategy and capital plan, giving investors a cleaner pure-play choice, and removing a conglomerate discount, where the market values the whole group at less than its parts. A well-known example is eBay spinning off PayPal in 2015. In India the same result is usually achieved through a demerger under an NCLT-sanctioned scheme. A spin-off differs from an equity carve-out, where shares in the unit are sold to new investors for cash, and from a sale to a buyer, where the parent receives cash and shareholders receive nothing directly.
example: Say ABC Ltd spins off its software unit at a ratio of 1 new share for every 4 ABC shares held. An investor with 2,000 ABC shares keeps them and also receives 500 shares of the new company.

short: The splitting off of a company's business into a separate company whose shares go to the original company's shareholders; India's usual route to a spin-off.
kid: A big toy box holds cars and dolls. You split it into two boxes, one for cars and one for dolls, and everyone who owned the big box now owns both small boxes.
detail: A demerger transfers one or more businesses of a company to a resulting company, which issues its shares to the demerged company's shareholders in an agreed ratio. Under India's Companies Act, 2013, it is carried out through a scheme of arrangement approved by shareholders and creditors and sanctioned by the NCLT, with listed companies first needing stock exchange and SEBI clearance. Shareholders usually end up owning two listed stocks, with the cost of their original shares split between them. Under the tax rules as of 2025, a demerger that meets set conditions, such as transferring all the unit's assets and liabilities and issuing shares proportionately, is tax-neutral. Recent examples include Reliance Industries demerging Jio Financial Services in 2023 and ITC demerging ITC Hotels, which listed in January 2025. It is broadly the Indian form of a spin-off, unlike a slump sale, where a business is sold for cash.
example: Say ABC Ltd demerges its retail arm into ABC Retail Ltd at a 1:1 ratio. A shareholder with 100 ABC shares worth ₹1,000 each before the record date might then hold 100 ABC shares worth ₹800 and 100 ABC Retail shares worth ₹200, so the total stays ₹1,00,000.

short: When a parent company sells a minority stake in one of its subsidiaries to outside investors, usually through an IPO, while keeping control.
kid: You own a whole cake. You sell a few slices to friends for coins but keep most of the cake for yourself.
detail: In an equity carve-out, a parent lists a subsidiary by selling part of its shares, often 10% to 30%, to the public in an IPO or to private investors, while keeping a controlling stake. Unlike a spin-off, it raises cash: for the subsidiary if new shares are issued, or for the parent if it sells existing shares through an offer for sale. It also creates a market price for the unit, which can highlight value hidden inside a conglomerate, and gives the subsidiary its own shares to use for acquisitions and employee stock options. A carve-out is often a first step toward full separation later. Indian groups have often used this route to list their insurance, asset management, card and finance subsidiaries. The risks include conflicts between the parent and minority shareholders, and the holding company discount investors may then apply to the parent.
example: Say ABC Ltd owns 100% of ABC Tech, valued at ₹5,000 crore, and sells 20% of it in an IPO through an offer for sale. ABC receives ₹1,000 crore in cash and still owns 80%, so it keeps control and continues to consolidate ABC Tech in its accounts.
